papers.title: AI-Native Industrial Control Systems: An Agent Architecture for the Control System Lifecycle
papers.abstract: Industrial control systems increasingly use AI for perception, control, and engineering, while available control functions and execution environments are typically established in advance. This paper proposes an AI-native industrial control system in which collaborating agents determine the capabilities required by a task, construct the control application, and prepare its execution environment. System-level agents coordinate device-level agents within configured resource and permission constraints. A physical sorting workstation illustrates two forms of adaptation. In the first case, controller and robot agents construct a sorting application on a prescribed Raspberry Pi target. In the second, a camera agent adds inspection on an edge node, and the controller associates inspection results with downstream pickup decisions. A subsequent revision enables selective sorting using the same agents and deployment arrangement. The trials demonstrate the feasibility of task-driven construction and evolution on the workstation. Commissioning also reveals limitations in the traceability of design decisions, adherence to delegated responsibilities, diagnostic reasoning, and verification of physical behavior.

papers.title: Particle physics science communication with grass-roots Instagram: a success story
papers.abstract: Communicating science to the public is an integral part of the work of a research collaboration, not an afterthought. Institutional and collaboration-level social media accounts are often run by professional communicators rather than by practising scientists, and single-scientist ``influencer'' accounts are demanding to sustain. We describe {\em CMSatDESY}, a crowd-sourced Instagram account on which the CMS group at DESY tells its own stories, each member in their own voice. In the first half of 2026, the science communication activities through this reached 140k+ unique accounts and received 250k+ views, with an engagement rate of 7\%. We discuss experiences and best practices that can be used by other groups, and describe how the account doubles as a science communication playground for outreach training for a large particle physics group.

papers.title: How Should Candidates Be Weighted under Open-List Proportional Representation? Harmonic Weights and Dirichlet Order Statistics
papers.abstract: Candidates in open-list proportional representation systems are not equally prominent, and measurements that involve aggregation over candidates therefore require some form of weighting. We address the question of how those weights should be chosen. Since weights based on realized preference votes are unavailable in advance and endogenous to the electoral outcome, we seek a priori weights that depend on list position alone, and derive them as expected ordered vote shares under a probabilistic model of the division of the list vote among candidates. The natural starting point -- the uniform distribution on the simplex -- is unrealistic, as it prescribes the same degree of concentration of the vote for every list, and under it the leading candidates become more alike as lists lengthen. The other members of the symmetric Dirichlet family require a concentration parameter, which is unknown and which there is no reason to expect to be constant across countries, parties, and elections. Accordingly, we treat that parameter as random. We prove that under a scale-invariant prior restricted to lists with at least two effective candidates, the expected share of the $k$-th candidate decays as $1/k$, and we show that over the leading positions of a long list, up to one hundred of them, the resulting weights are within 1.4 to 3.4 percent, in total variation, of the harmonic weights $(k H_n)^{-1}$, where $H_n$ is the $n$-th harmonic number. No fixed value of the parameter yields similar weights. Moreover, under the uniform distribution itself, harmonic weights are exactly the normalized expected margins between consecutive candidates.

papers.title: Neckpinches in a Positively Curved Market: Ricci Flow with Surgery on the Nikkei-225
papers.abstract: We study the intrinsic geometry of the Nikkei-225 through the discrete Ollivier-Ricci curvature (ORC) of its empirical correlation graph, using the graph Ricci flow and surgery methodology of arXiv:2510.15942. The 226-node correlation graph, built from daily returns between January 2020 and June 2026, is ORC-spherical: every edge has strictly positive curvature before any flow, close to the equal-weight value $\kappa\approx0.502$. Under a fixed 20-iteration Ricci flow the curvature distribution polarises into a high-curvature bulk and a low-curvature minority, and cutting the low-curvature edges splits the graph into components of 184 and 42 nodes. The recursive ARCUS procedure (Adaptive Ricci Curvature Unsupervised Surgery) stops the flow at each node once a curvature gap ratio $G$ exceeds $G_{\min}$ and the surgery set is stable. With $G_{\min}=10$ and a minimum cluster size of 15, ARCUS performs 28 surgeries over 13 levels and ends in 29 terminal clusters of 2-14 nodes. The stopping rule fires at every node, with $G$ between 10.0 and 92.4, and the top-level split reproduces the fixed-schedule 184/42 partition exactly. Eight small subgraphs stop with $G<15$, so the deeper levels are conditional on $G_{\min}$. Many terminal clusters are single industries by inspection, among them nine banks, five insurers, five general trading companies, three steelmakers and three shipping lines. Two delisted stocks without price data enter as zero-correlation placeholders; with them excluded, every terminal cluster is more strongly correlated internally than with the rest of the index.
